Uncertainty of spatial averages and totals

A Python implementation of Wadoux & Heuvelink (2023): parity with the authors’ R script, verification on synthetic truth, and ablations

Published

October 13, 2026

Summary

This report documents pyspatialuncertainty, a Python implementation of the Monte Carlo method of Wadoux & Heuvelink (2023). The method estimates the uncertainty of spatial averages and totals of maps. The report also covers a per-class extension for maps of calibrated class probabilities. Its main findings:

Parity with the authors’ R script.

  • The R script was run unchanged apart from two RStudio-only lines, and its intermediates were exported.
  • On those inputs, the Python standardized errors, sample variogram and correlogram all match R. So does the integrand on the script’s own 1,000 Monte Carlo pairs, to within 4e-16.
  • Python’s Monte Carlo estimate of the block variance with m = 10⁶ pairs is 0.09824 ± 0.00009. R gives 0.09808 ± 0.00009 with m = 10⁶ and 0.09798 with the script’s m = 1,000. The differences are 1.2 and 0.1 combined Monte Carlo standard errors.

Verification on synthetic truth (continuous maps).

  • The scenario has known non-stationary σ and known correlated errors. With the true σ and correlation, the Monte Carlo estimate matches the exact block SD (median ratio 1.000 for 8 × 8-cell blocks).
  • In that oracle case, 90 % intervals cover the truth 90 % of the time for 8 × 8 blocks.
  • With a correlogram fitted to 300 validation errors, coverage is 90 % for 8 × 8 blocks and 84 % for the whole domain. For large blocks, errors in the long-range part of the fitted correlogram dominate.

The two naive alternatives fail as the paper warns.

  • Averaging point SDs overstates the block SD by up to 7.5 times, at the domain scale.
  • Assuming independent errors understates it by a factor of up to 16, and 90 % intervals then cover only 8 %.

The method carries any error in σ straight into the result. The correlogram is normalised by its sill, so the method trusts σ for scale. Scaling σ by c scales the block SD by c. Coverage falls to 59 % for c = 0.5 and rises to 100 % for c = 2. The fitted sill of the standardized errors (≈ 1/c²) is the diagnostic. In the authors’ example it is 0.65.

The categorical and pipeline results are in Section 3.2 and Section 3.3.

1 Methods

1.1 The method of Wadoux & Heuvelink (2023)

Let ε(s) be the point-support prediction error of a map. For a block B (Eq. 7 of the paper),

var⁡(1|B|∫Bε(s)ds)=1|B|2∫B∫Bσ(s)σ(u)ρ(|s−u|)dsdu. \operatorname{var}\Big(\frac{1}{|B|}\int_B \varepsilon(s)\,ds\Big) = \frac{1}{|B|^2}\int_B\int_B \sigma(s)\,\sigma(u)\,\rho(|s-u|)\,ds\,du .

The two ingredients are:

  • σ(s), the point-support prediction-error SD. It comes from the predictive distribution of any mapping model, e.g. a quantile regression forest (QRF).
  • ρ(h), the correlation function of the standardized errors ε/σ. It comes from a variogram fitted to standardized cross-validation errors, using ρ(h) = (sill − γ(h))/sill.

The double integral equals E[σ(S)σ(U)ρ(|S − U|)] for independent uniform points S, U in B. It is estimated by averaging over m pairs, with m = 10,000 in the paper and 1,000 in the R script. The variance of the block total is |B|² times that of the block average, and normal prediction intervals follow from the central limit theorem.

1.2 Categorical extension

For class k with calibrated probability pkp_k and indicator IkI_k, the procedure is the same as above:

  1. Error and SD. The error is ek=Ik−pke_k = I_k - p_k, with σk=pk(1−pk)\sigma_k = \sqrt{p_k(1-p_k)}.
  2. Correlogram. One correlogram is fitted per class to the standardized errors ek/σke_k/\sigma_k at validation points.
  3. Integral. The integral is evaluated as above, with all classes sharing the same point pairs.
  4. Predictions. The expected fraction is the block mean of pkp_k, and the expected area is |B||B| times that. Intervals are clipped to [0, 1].

Probabilities that do not sum to one, or that are exactly 0 or 1, are rejected. Only marginal per-class uncertainty is modelled.

1.3 Implementation

Component Choice
Variograms Own implementation following gstat. Models Nug, Exp, Sph, Gau, Mat, Ste use gstat’s range parameter. Sample variograms use cutoff = 0.33333 × bbox diagonal and width = cutoff/15, with upper-inclusive lag classes. WLS uses fit.method 1/2/6/7.
Automatic fitting (experiments) Nug + {Exp, Sph, Gau}, 4 starting ranges each, best weighted SSE, fit.method = 7. Practical range is bounded by 2× the largest lag and partial sills by 2× the largest γ̂. This is the paper’s procedure, fit_correlation(method="wls").
Package default for step 4 Since this report was produced, fit_correlation and fit_class_variograms default to a Gaussian maximum-likelihood fit of Nug + {Exp, Sph, Gau} with the error mean fixed at zero. This report verifies the paper’s WLS procedure. experiments/improvements/ in the repository compares the two on the same kind of simulations.
Blocks Tiles, zones, polygons, boxes or the whole domain. Polygons and boxes are sampled exactly (rejection sampling, as spatstat::runifpoint). σ is looked up in the containing cell, as raster::extract.
Monte Carlo Paired estimator with MCSE = sd(g)/√m. One RNG stream per block. Pairs are shared across classes and estimators.
Data structures xarray/rioxarray rasters (projected CRS), Polars 2.0.0 tables.

1.4 Verification design

Parity with R. The authors’ script (AlexandreWadoux/UncertaintySpatialAggregation@934481f) ran under R 4.3.3 with gstat 2.1-1, ranger 0.16.0, raster 3.6-26 and spatstat 3.0-7. A harness re-drew the script’s Monte Carlo pairs from the saved RNG state and asserted bit-identical results. Python consumed the exported intermediates, because R’s random streams and ranger cannot be reproduced exactly in Python.

Synthetic truth. The method targets the continuous block average. The synthetic fields are therefore simulated on a sub-grid with 4 × 4 nodes per map cell, and the true block value is the sub-grid mean. Point-scale nugget variation enters only the point observations, which are the validation data. Fields are drawn exactly by FFT circulant embedding.

Scenario Truth What the method receives
Continuous errors (ErrorModelScenario) 128 × 128 cells. Errors σ(s)·ε*(s), with σ ∈ [0.5, 2] non-stationary and ε* = nugget + exponential(range a). Baseline: a = 8 cells, nugget 0.25. c·σ, and 300 validation errors
Class maps (LatentClassScenario) A latent μ(s) + η(s) thresholded into 3 classes (≈ 60/30/10 %). η = nugget + exponential noise. Signal-to-noise Var(μ)/Var(η). Exactly calibrated p (optionally temperature-scaled), and 300 validation labels
Full pipeline (PipelineScenario) The R script’s design: trend + GRF 5·exp(−h/25) on [0, 100]², 200 samples. Ranger-style QRF predictions and σ, and 10-fold CV errors

Estimators. The same four are compared throughout:

  • method: the paper’s procedure with a fitted correlogram;
  • oracle: the true σ and correlation; for class maps, the exact domain-averaged correlogram of the standardized indicator errors;
  • naive_avg: the mean of σ over the block;
  • naive_indep: √Σσ²/n.

Metrics. For each configuration, 500 realizations (baseline) or 300 (ablations) were run. The metrics are:

  • coverage of 50/80/90/95 % normal intervals, with 95 % CIs from a cluster bootstrap over realizations;
  • SD ratio, the RMS of the estimated SD over realizations divided by the true SD. The true SD is the brute-force RMS of the block errors, and is also checked against the exact value where one is available.

2 Parity with the authors’ R script

The R script’s results for the whole domain:

  • block mean prediction 12.913;
  • block SD 0.3130;
  • 90 % interval [12.400, 13.426], which contains the true mean 12.906.

The same function in Python, given the same inputs, reproduces these within Monte Carlo error. The test suite also checks gstat’s fitted parameters for fit.method 1, 6 and 7 (agreement to about 10⁻⁴) and gstat’s variogramLine for every supported model.

The spread of the Monte Carlo estimate shrinks as 1/m1/\sqrt{m}. Half the 90 % range of the estimated SD is 2.4 % of its value at the script’s m = 1,000, and 0.8 % at the paper’s m = 10,000. The package reports the Monte Carlo standard error with every estimate, so users can choose m deliberately.

3 Verification on synthetic truth

3.1 Continuous maps

Oracle. With the true σ and correlation, the Monte Carlo estimate agrees with the exact block SD, computed by FFT on the sub-grid, at every block size. The coverage of every interval level matches its nominal value. So the integration, the block geometry and the definition of the truth are mutually consistent.

Fitted correlogram. The method is close to nominal for blocks up to about 16 × 16 cells. Coverage falls for the largest blocks, to 84 % for the whole domain, even though the median SD ratio stays near 1 (0.98). The cause is variability, not bias. The domain-scale variance depends on the long-range part of the correlogram, which 300 validation points pin down poorly. In some realizations the SD is much too small, and those intervals miss.

3.2 Class probability maps

For 8 × 8-cell blocks, the fitted method’s 90 % intervals have this coverage:

class a (≈ 60 %) class b (≈ 30 %) class c (≈ 10 %, rare)
method coverage 88 % 83 % 81 %
method SD ratio 1.00 1.02 1.21
oracle coverage 92 % 92 % 92 %

The oracle uses the exact domain-averaged correlogram. Comparing it with the truth shows how much is lost by assuming a stationary correlation of the standardized indicator errors. For a thresholded latent field, that correlation really depends on the probabilities at both locations. Comparing the method with the oracle shows the additional cost of estimating one correlogram per class from 300 binary observations. For the rare class, few validation points carry a positive indicator, so its correlogram is the hardest to estimate. For the whole domain, even the oracle covers only 78 % for the rare class, and 88 % for class a. There the stationary approximation itself is the limiting factor.

3.3 The R example as a full pipeline

In the Python port, the median variance of the standardized CV errors is 0.54. For the authors’ own realization it is 0.63, and their hand-set variogram sill is 0.65. Ranger’s quantile regression forest makes σ too wide by a factor of about 1/√0.6 ≈ 1.3. The faithful method normalises the variogram, so it carries this over-dispersion into the block SDs.

Correlogram fitting interacts with this. For tiles, the automatic single-structure fit decays faster than the true error correlation, which roughly offsets the wide σ: the median SD ratio is 0.95 for 25 × 25-node tiles. But the fitted correlogram varies between realizations, and coverage falls short at 83 %. The R script’s nested model, with its ranges fixed and its sills fitted, keeps the weak long-range structures and so gives larger SDs: a median ratio of 1.30 and coverage of 91 % for the same tiles. For the whole domain, both over-estimate the SD (median ratios 1.5 and 3.8), with coverage of 92 % and 98 %. In short, the over-dispersed QRF σ and the uncertain long-range correlation dominate the accuracy of the end-to-end pipeline.

4 Ablations

Each ablation changes one factor relative to the baseline. The panels show the fitted method for four block sizes. The tables give coverage pooled over all tiles for every estimator, including the naive baselines.

4.1 Continuous maps

Misspecified σ. The block SD scales with the σ that the method receives, and coverage follows. The fitted sill of the standardized errors reveals the problem: its median is 3.99 when σ is halved and 0.25 when σ is doubled, against 1 when calibrated. Passing a constant σ in place of the true non-stationary one has a milder effect.

Correlation range.

  • Very short ranges (1 cell). The first lag class of the default sample variogram (cutoff/15 ≈ 4 cells) is too coarse to resolve them. The fitted correlogram is wrong in both directions: too low for the smallest blocks and too high for the largest.
  • Very long ranges (64 cells, practical range 192 on a 128-cell domain). The sample variogram never reaches its sill within the cutoff. The sill-normalised correlogram then underestimates the correlation, and large blocks are under-covered.

Nugget. With a nugget share of 0.9, 16 % of the fits are pure nugget. The paper’s continuous integral is then exactly zero, and coverage collapses for those realizations. This is a property of the faithful method: a pure-nugget correlogram implies that the errors average out completely.

Number of validation points. More validation points give better correlograms, and coverage moves towards nominal.

4.2 Class probability maps

Miscalibration. Temperature scaling biases both inputs: the expected fractions and σ_k. Over-confident probabilities (T < 1) shrink σ_k = sqrt(p(1 − p)) where the probabilities are sharp. Under-confident ones (T > 1) inflate it and also bias the expected areas of rare classes upwards. Coverage reflects both effects. Even the oracle, which uses the calibrated σ_k, loses coverage under miscalibration (see the table), because the expected fractions it is centred on are biased. As in the continuous case, the fitted sill of the standardized indicator errors flags the problem.

Signal-to-noise, range and nugget. Higher signal-to-noise gives sharper probabilities, so smaller σ_k and fewer validation points near the class boundaries. The latent range and nugget act much as in the continuous case, except that the indicator transform makes the effective correlation shorter and weaker than the latent correlation.

4.3 The R-example pipeline

5 Discussion and limitations

  • Implementation. The core computation is right. Given the same inputs, the package reproduces the authors’ R script exactly where the computation is deterministic and within Monte Carlo error where it is stochastic. With the true σ and correlation it recovers exact block variances at every scale.
  • Where the uncertainty comes from. The method’s accuracy in practice depends almost entirely on its inputs: the calibration of σ and the quality of the fitted correlogram.
    • The sill normalisation in step 4 discards the one statistic that would reveal a mis-scaled σ. Reporting the fitted sill alongside the block SDs is cheap and should be routine.
    • For large blocks, the weak long-range part of the correlogram dominates, and it is the part a sample variogram estimates worst. Analyst judgement, such as the nested model in the R script, matters.
  • Nugget and support. The estimator targets continuous block averages, so a nugget contributes nothing. That is right for micro-scale variation and measurement error. It is not right if the quantity of interest is the mean of a finite set of point values. The synthetic truth used here is consistent with the paper’s estimand.
  • Categorical mode.
    • It keeps the continuous machinery but relies on a stationary correlogram of standardized indicator errors. That is an approximation, and its quality depends on class prevalence and the sharpness of the probabilities.
    • Only marginal per-class uncertainty is provided.
    • Probabilities must be calibrated. Temperature-scaled (miscalibrated) probabilities distort both the expected areas and their uncertainty.
  • Scope. Not covered: geographic coordinates, which need reprojecting; bounded or skewed intervals; and cross-class dependence.

Software: pyspatialuncertainty 1.0.0, numpy 2.5.4, scipy 1.18.1, xarray 2026.9.0, rioxarray 0.23.0, polars 2.0.0, shapely 2.2.0, scikit-learn 1.9.1. Reference R run: R version 4.3.3 (2024-02-29).
